screens.title: Advanced Role Techniques: Arguments, Conditionals, and Includes
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on making roles adaptable and safe for real environments. You will learn how to pass variables as arguments so a single role can behave differently per environment, use conditional logic to run only the tasks that make sense for a host, and decide when to include a role statically at parse time or dynamically at run time. These techniques let you avoid editing role internals just to change behavior, reduce duplication, and surface errors earlier when you use static imports. You will also see how blocks, rescue, and always provide structured error handling inside role tasks, and how pre_tasks and post_tasks help with global setup or cleanup independent of role internals. For example, a webserver role can expose a port variable that you override per-playbook or per-role invocation so the same role deploys to production and development without code changes. By the end of the module you will know practical trade-offs for import_role versus include_role and how to combine conditions and blocks to make robust playbooks. Consider how these patterns make automation more maintainable and testable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Overview
Advanced Role Techniques
Make roles reusable across environments with arguments, conditionals, and controlled inclusion.

This chapter teaches patterns that let a single role adapt to many situations. You will pass role arguments to override defaults, guard tasks and roles with when conditions, and decide between import_role for static safety and include_role for runtime flexibility. Blocks and pre/post tasks give structured control over multi-step operations and cleanup.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Pass Arguments: override defaults at invocation
Conditionals: run tasks only when conditions are true
Includes: static import vs dynamic include
Explore Key Topics
Role Arguments
Override defaults per-playbook or per-role call to tune behavior without editing role files.
Conditionals
Use when on tasks, blocks, and role includes to adapt to OS facts and runtime data.
Include Types
import_role is parsed statically. include_role runs at execution time and supports loops.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to pass arguments into roles so a single role can support multiple environments, add conditional logic to tasks and role invocation to run only the steps you need, and explain the difference between include_role and import_role to choose the right inclusion strategy. You will also learn to structure complex role interactions with blocks, using rescue and always for error handling, and to use pre_tasks and post_tasks for global setup and teardown. For example, you will pass a port value into a webserver role at playbook time to deploy the same role to both development and production, you will write when conditions that check ansible_os_family to install the correct package per operating system, and you will use include_role inside a loop to deploy multiple applications with different parameters. These skills reduce duplication and let you keep roles generic while controlling behavior from the playbook level.

screens.title: Passing Arguments to Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Passing arguments into a role means supplying variables at the point you call that role so it behaves differently without editing its defaults. This keeps a role generic and reusable. A common pattern is to set sensible values in defaults/main. yml and then override them either at the playbook vars level or inline when you declare the role. For example, a webserver role might have nginx_port in defaults set to a safe default, but a production playbook sets that variable to 443 at the play level or a development playbook passes 8080 directly with role: webserver nginx_port: 8080. The difference matters: play-level vars affect the whole play, while inline role args target only that role execution. A misconception is to duplicate roles instead of overriding variables; duplication increases maintenance cost. A small concrete example shows how to pass nginx_port directly in a role entry. Practice this with environment-specific values and remember variable precedence — play or role invocation variables override defaults. Question to consider: how would you troubleshoot a role if the expected override is not applied? Passing Arguments to Roles means use role invocation variables to configure behavior per run and avoid changing role internals.. In practical terms, how to override defaults and tailor a role per invocation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Role-level configuration
keyIdea.text: Use role invocation variables to configure behavior per run and avoid changing role internals.

content.html:
Core Concept
Pass Arguments to Roles
Override default variables at invocation to customize role behavior without changing role files.
Why this matters
  • Keeps a single role reusable across environments.
  • Reduces duplication and maintenance burden.
  • Allows targeted configuration per role call.
Common mistake
Duplicating roles to change behavior instead of passing arguments creates drift and extra upkeep.
Key Takeaway

Pass configuration via role args or play vars to keep roles generic and reusable across targets.

Concrete examples
# deploy_prod_webserver.yml
- name: Deploy production web server
  hosts: prod_webservers
  become: true
  vars:
    nginx_port: 443
  roles:
    - webserver

# deploy_dev_webserver.yml
- name: Deploy development web server
  hosts: dev_webservers
  become: true
  roles:
    - role: webserver
      nginx_port: 8080
The second example shows a role-level argument set only for that invocation. If a value isn’t applied as expected, check variable precedence and where the variable was defined.
Try this
Create a role with a default port and override it from two playbooks to see how the role behaves.

screens.title: Variable Precedence and Scope
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding where a variable comes from is essential to predict role behavior. Ansible applies variable precedence rules so values defined closer to execution override broader defaults. A role’s defaults are intentionally low-precedence so a playbook can override them without changing the role. You can set variables at the play level, inventory, extra-vars, or pass them on the role line. For instance, defaults/main. yml might set service_state to started, but a playbook or inline role invocation can set service_state to stopped for a particular run. A practical misconception is expecting defaults to win; they are the lowest priority. When troubleshooting, examine where the variable was defined and whether an extra-vars value or play-level var is shadowing it. In complex projects, documenting which variables are intended to be overridden helps other authors. A concrete walkthrough uses the flexible_service role defaults and the test playbook to show how install_package and service_name change the role's actions. Variable Precedence and Scope means role defaults are lowest precedence; play or invocation vars override them to shape runtime behavior.. In practical terms, defaults, play vars, and role-level overrides. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Know precedence
keyIdea.text: Role defaults are lowest precedence; play or invocation vars override them to shape runtime behavior.

content.html:
Definition
Variable Precedence and Scope
Defaults are intentionally overridden by playbook and invocation variables so roles remain flexible.
Checklist when a value is unexpected
  • Check if the variable exists in defaults/main.yml inside the role.
  • Look for play-level vars or inline args that override the default.
  • Remember extra-vars have highest precedence; use them deliberately for test runs.
A good practice is to keep role defaults minimal and document which values you expect callers to override. This reduces surprises when multiple authors use the same role.
Example: role defaults
# flexible_service/defaults/main.yml
---
service_name: "nginx"
service_state: "started"
service_enabled: true
install_package: true
Playbook override
# test_flexible_service.yml (excerpt)
- name: Include flexible_service role for Apache
  ansible.builtin.include_role:
    name: flexible_service
  vars:
    service_name: "apache2"
    service_state: "stopped"
    install_package: false
This example shows how role defaults are replaced by variables supplied at the role invocation. If the service remains in the old state, check for another higher-precedence value defining the same variable.

screens.title: Conditional Logic inside Roles with when
screens.narratorSegment: Conditional logic is the primary tool to adapt tasks to the target environment. The when statement can be applied to single tasks, to whole blocks, or when including a role. A common use is branching on ansible_os_family to install the correct package name for the platform. You can also conditionally enable features, for example running firewall configuration only if firewall_enabled is truthy. A common misconception is to rely on implicit assumptions about facts; always validate the fact key you use. When combined with defaults and role arguments, when gives you precise control: a role can accept a variable feature_enabled and skip feature setup when false. A concrete example shows three tasks: installing nginx on Debian, installing on RedHat, and configuring a firewall only when a flag is set. If you see both package tasks attempting to run, check that your when expressions are correct and that facts are gathered or available. Closing question: how would you test conditionals in a CI environment where facts might differ? Conditional Logic inside Roles with when means use when everywhere needed so roles run only the tasks appropriate to each host's facts and configuration.. In practical terms, use host facts and variables to run tasks selectively. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Guard role behavior
keyIdea.text: Use when everywhere needed so roles run only the tasks appropriate to each host's facts and configuration.

content.html:
Process Flow
Conditional Logic with when
Use facts and variables to choose which tasks run. Verify facts are present and correct.
Tips
  • Use explicit fact checks like ansible_os_family == "Debian".
  • Provide default values for optional flags to avoid undefined errors.
  • Test conditionals with fact overrides in development inventories.
Common pitfall
Missing facts cause unexpected task execution; ensure gather_facts is enabled or provide fact fallbacks.
Example tasks
- name: Install Nginx on Debian-based systems
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: nginx
    state: present
  when: ansible_os_family == "Debian"

- name: Install Nginx on RedHat-based systems
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: nginx
    state: present
  when: ansible_os_family == "RedHat"

- name: Configure firewall for Nginx (if enabled)
  ansible.posix.firewalld:
    port: "{{ nginx_port }}/tcp"
    state: enabled
    permanent: true
    immediate: true
  when: firewall_enabled | default(false)
This shows precise conditions. If firewall_enabled is not defined, the task will be skipped because of the default filter. That default pattern prevents errors when a variable isn't provided.

screens.title: Guarding Role Execution with when
screens.narratorSegment: You can apply conditional logic not only to tasks but to the invocation of roles themselves. Putting a when on a role in the roles list or on an include_role allows you to skip entire role runs when preconditions aren't met. This is useful for toggling features across environments or preventing an expensive role from running on control nodes. A typical pattern is to set deploy_app: true in a playbook and then attach the when to the role invocation so the role is executed only when requested. A common misunderstanding is to believe conditions on roles behave exactly like task-level when clauses; role-level when checks whether to include the whole role, while task-level when controls individual steps inside the role. For orchestration, use role-level when when you want to avoid evaluating or loading a role at all. As an exercise, try adding a when: deploy_app condition to a role invocation and verify that tasks inside the role do not run when the condition is false. Guarding Role Execution with when means applying when to role invocation prevents a role from being loaded or executed when conditions are not met.. In practical terms, skip or include roles based on variables and host facts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Role-level guards
keyIdea.text: Applying when to role invocation prevents a role from being loaded or executed when conditions are not met.

content.html:
Definition
Role-level conditional execution
Use when on a role to avoid loading or executing it unless necessary.
Why use this
  • Skip expensive operations when not required.
  • Keep playbooks clearer by enabling features declaratively.
  • Prevent role tasks from running on inappropriate hosts.
Example: conditional role invocation
- name: Deploy application conditionally
  hosts: webservers
  become: true
  vars:
    deploy_app: true
  roles:
    - role: app_deploy
      when: deploy_app
If deploy_app is false or undefined, the app_deploy role is skipped entirely. This is a clean way to gate large changes without modifying the role itself.
Key Takeaway

Use role-level when to conditionally include roles and avoid unnecessary task evaluation.

screens.title: import_role vs include_role
screens.narratorSegment: A key design decision is picking import_role or include_role. import_role is static: Ansible processes it at parse time and effectively inlines the role's tasks into the playbook before execution begins. That means syntax errors surface early and the full task list is known ahead of running plays. It’s appropriate for predictable, fixed dependencies where you don’t need runtime decisions. include_role is dynamic: it is processed at runtime and allows looped inclusion and conditional logic evaluated during execution. That makes it the right tool when you need to include the same role multiple times with different arguments, or include depending on runtime facts. A common pitfall is using include_role when a static import would be safer; this can delay failure detection until execution reaches the include. A concrete scenario where include_role is necessary is when looping over multiple app specs and including the same role per item with different parameters for each application. When choosing, weigh early error detection and predictability versus runtime flexibility. import_role vs include_role means use import_role for static, predictable includes; use include_role when you need runtime decisions or loops.. In practical terms, static parse-time embedding vs runtime inclusion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Static vs dynamic inclusion
keyIdea.text: Use import_role for static, predictable includes; use include_role when you need runtime decisions or loops.

content.html:
Comparison
import_role vs include_role
Understand the timing difference: parse time versus runtime.
Import (static)
  • Processed at parse time.
  • Errors surface before execution.
  • Good for predictable dependencies.
Include (dynamic)
  • Processed at runtime.
  • Supports loops and runtime variables.
  • Errors may appear only when executed.
Example: static import
- name: Statically import a role
  ansible.builtin.import_role:
    name: common_setup
  vars:
    message: "This is from static import"
Example: dynamic include with loop
- name: Dynamically include a role based on a loop
  ansible.builtin.include_role:
    name: config_app
  loop:
    - app_name: frontend
      app_port: 80
    - app_name: backend
      app_port: 8080
  loop_control:
    loop_var: current_app
  vars:
    app_name: "{{ current_app.app_name }}"
    app_port: "{{ current_app.app_port }}"
The looped include lets you run the same role per item with different parameters; import_role cannot be looped this way at parse time.

screens.title: Dynamic Inclusion with include_role and Loops
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic inclusion shines when you must apply the same role multiple times with different parameters. include_role evaluated at runtime can be placed inside a task loop, letting you pass per-item vars by using loop_control and a loop variable. For example, you could loop over application specifications and include the deploy_app role for each app, setting app_name and app_port from the loop item. This pattern is ideal when the number of items or their configuration is not known until execution, or when each item needs slight variations. A misconception is trying to use import_role in a loop; static import is evaluated before the loop context exists and will not give you per-item behavior. When using include_role in loops, be mindful of idempotence and variable scoping, and prefer explicit loop_var names to avoid accidental overwrites. Try this pattern to deploy two apps with different ports using the same role and verify each run receives its own variables during execution. Dynamic Inclusion with include_role and Loops means use include_role within a loop to invoke a role multiple times with different arguments for each item.. In practical terms, deploy multiple items by including the same role per iteration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Per-item role runs
keyIdea.text: Use include_role within a loop to invoke a role multiple times with different arguments for each item.

content.html:
Process Flow
Include role in a loop
Runtime inclusion supports per-item configuration and dynamic counts.
Best practices
  • Use explicit loop_var to avoid variable collisions.
  • Keep the role idempotent so repeated includes are safe.
  • Test with representative loop items in a dry-run scenario first.
Practical looped include
- name: Dynamically include a role based on a loop
  ansible.builtin.include_role:
    name: config_app
  loop:
    - app_name: frontend
      app_port: 80
    - app_name: backend
      app_port: 8080
  loop_control:
    loop_var: current_app
  vars:
    app_name: "{{ current_app.app_name }}"
    app_port: "{{ current_app.app_port }}"
Each iteration runs the role with the variables set from the current loop item. This pattern is commonly used to deploy or configure multiple applications using one reusable role.

screens.title: Blocks, rescue, and always for Error Handling
screens.narratorSegment: Blocks let you group tasks that share common attributes and provide structured error handling. Within a block you can declare multiple tasks that should run together, and then attach rescue and always sections. If any task in the block fails, the rescue section runs to handle errors, and the always section runs regardless of success or failure. This pattern is helpful for deployment workflows where a partial failure requires logging, rollback, or cleanup. A typical misconception is expecting rescue tasks to retry the failed task automatically; rescue is for handling, not automatic retries. Use explicit debugging or corrective steps in rescue. The example deploy application block shows creating directories, copying binaries, and starting services. If a copy fails, the rescue can log the failure and ensure temporary files are cleaned in always. This makes roles more resilient and predictable in real infrastructure. keyIdea.title: Controlled failure handling
keyIdea.text: Use block with rescue and always to handle partial failures and ensure cleanup runs reliably.

content.html:
Process Flow
Blocks with rescue and always
Group related tasks and provide explicit error handling paths and guaranteed cleanup.
When to use
  • Multi-step deployments where partial success needs handling.
  • Ensuring cleanup tasks run even on failure.
  • Logging and reporting of failures in a consistent place.
Example block
- name: Deploy application components
  ansible.builtin.block:
    - name: Create application directory
      ansible.builtin.file:
        path: /opt/my_app
        state: directory
        mode: '0755'

    - name: Copy application binary
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        src: my_app_binary
        dest: /opt/my_app/my_app
        mode: '0755'

    - name: Start application service
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: my_app
        state: started
        enabled: true
  rescue:
    - name: Log deployment failure
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "Application deployment failed for {{ inventory_hostname }}"
  always:
    - name: Clean up temporary files
      ansible.builtin.file:
        path: /tmp/app_temp_files
        state: absent
Use rescue to react to failure and always for cleanup. Remember rescue won't automatically retry tasks; design retries intentionally if required.

screens.title: pre_tasks and post_tasks
screens.narratorSegment: pre_tasks and post_tasks provide a way to run global setup or teardown steps around role execution. pre_tasks execute before any roles or regular tasks, which makes them suitable for environment preparation like ensuring required packages or fetching credentials. post_tasks run after all roles and regular tasks, which is useful for cleanup, reporting, or collecting logs. A misconception is that pre_tasks replace role responsibilities; they are complementary. Use pre_tasks for global concerns that apply across roles, and keep role internals focused on their specific service domain. For example, a pre_task might ensure a package repository is configured before roles that install packages run, and a post_task might collect status or remove temporary credentials. keyIdea.title: End-to-end example
keyIdea.text: The flexible_service role shows role defaults, conditional installation, and role invocation with per-call variables.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Flexible Service Role
Define defaults, conditionals, and call the role with different parameters to observe behavior.
Why this exercise
  • See variable overrides in action.
  • Validate conditional installation and service management.
  • Practice include_role invocation with guard conditions.
Key files (excerpt)
# flexible_service/defaults/main.yml
---
service_name: "nginx"
service_state: "started"
service_enabled: true
install_package: true

# flexible_service/tasks/main.yml
---
- name: Ensure service package is installed (if requested)
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: "{{ service_name }}"
    state: present
  when: install_package

- name: Ensure service is in desired state and enabled
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: "{{ service_name }}"
    state: "{{ service_state }}"
    enabled: "{{ service_enabled }}"

# test_flexible_service.yml (excerpt)
- name: Include flexible_service role for Nginx
  ansible.builtin.include_role:
    name: flexible_service
  vars:
    service_name: "nginx"
    service_state: "started"
    install_package: true
Run the provided playbook and confirm service states. Adjust variables to see how the role adapts without editing its tasks.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: When applying these advanced role techniques, watch for common pitfalls. One frequent mistake is duplicating a role for environment differences rather than passing arguments; duplication increases maintenance and leads to inconsistent behavior. Another is forgetting variable precedence — assuming defaults override play vars when the opposite is true — so document intended override points. Choosing include_role when you don't need runtime flexibility can hide syntax errors until execution; prefer import_role for stable, known dependencies because it surfaces parse-time problems. Also avoid placing expensive operations inside repeated includes without idempotence checks. When using when conditions, ensure the facts you reference are available; for example, gather_facts must be on or you must supply the needed facts. Best practices: keep roles focused, document overridable variables in defaults with comments, prefer import_role for static dependencies, and use include_role for per-item loops or runtime decisions. Ask yourself as you design: can a caller decide this behavior without editing role internals? keyIdea.title: Design for maintainability
keyIdea.text: Prefer overriding variables to duplication, choose import_role for static needs, and test conditionals and includes carefully.

content.html:
Common Mistakes
Avoid these pitfalls
  • Duplicating roles instead of overriding variables creates drift.
  • Using include_role when import_role would reveal errors earlier.
  • Referencing facts that aren’t gathered or defined, causing unexpected behavior.
  • Placing non-idempotent actions inside repeated includes without guards.
Best practices
  • Document overridable variables in defaults with clear intent.
  • Prefer static imports for predictable dependencies and early error detection.
  • Use include_role for per-item or runtime-dependent needs, and keep roles idempotent.
  • Test conditionals with representative facts in CI or staging.
Pro Tip

Keep variable names explicit and avoid collision by scoping role variables with clear prefixes when necessary.

screens.title: Key Concepts

Third, import_role is parsed statically while include_role executes at runtime; choose between early error detection and runtime flexibility depending on your needs. Keeping these principles in mind helps you write modular, maintainable automation: define safe defaults in roles, override them at the play or role invocation level, guard behavior with conditionals, and use inclusion types that match your orchestration needs. A short mental checklist before you finalize a playbook: can a caller change behavior with variables, are your conditions explicit, and is your inclusion type appropriate for the operation?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on making roles adaptable and safe for real environments. You will learn how to pass variables as arguments so a single role can behave differently per environment, use conditional logic to run only the tasks that make sense for a host, and decide when to include a role statically at parse time or dynamically at run time. These techniques let you avoid editing role internals just to change behavior, reduce duplication, and surface errors earlier when you use static imports. You will also see how blocks, rescue, and always provide structured error handling inside role tasks, and how pre_tasks and post_tasks help with global setup or cleanup independent of role internals. For example, a webserver role can expose a port variable that you override per-playbook or per-role invocation so the same role deploys to production and development without code changes. By the end of the module you will know practical trade-offs for import_role versus include_role and how to combine conditions and blocks to make robust playbooks. Consider how these patterns make automation more maintainable and testable.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to pass arguments into roles so a single role can support multiple environments, add conditional logic to tasks and role invocation to run only the steps you need, and explain the difference between include_role and import_role to choose the right inclusion strategy. You will also learn to structure complex role interactions with blocks, using rescue and always for error handling, and to use pre_tasks and post_tasks for global setup and teardown. For example, you will pass a port value into a webserver role at playbook time to deploy the same role to both development and production, you will write when conditions that check ansible_os_family to install the correct package per operating system, and you will use include_role inside a loop to deploy multiple applications with different parameters. These skills reduce duplication and let you keep roles generic while controlling behavior from the playbook level.

This second objectives slide emphasizes how you'll apply the techniques. You'll practice passing role-specific variables both at the play level and directly on a role invocation so you experience precedence and scope. You'll write when conditions that use host facts such as ansible_os_family to conditionally install packages or enable services. You will construct a playbook that uses include_role inside a loop to configure multiple applications with different parameters, showing why dynamic inclusion is the right tool for per-item configuration. Finally, you'll assemble a role that uses a block with rescue and always sections to handle failures and cleanup reliably. These tasks are practical: passing a port to a webserver role, conditionally installing httpd or apache2 depending on OS family, and looping include_role to deploy frontend and backend applications. Each exercise reinforces how these patterns make automation safer and more modular.

Passing arguments into a role means supplying variables at the point you call that role so it behaves differently without editing its defaults. This keeps a role generic and reusable. A common pattern is to set sensible values in defaults/main. yml and then override them either at the playbook vars level or inline when you declare the role. For example, a webserver role might have nginx_port in defaults set to a safe default, but a production playbook sets that variable to 443 at the play level or a development playbook passes 8080 directly with role: webserver nginx_port: 8080. The difference matters: play-level vars affect the whole play, while inline role args target only that role execution. A misconception is to duplicate roles instead of overriding variables; duplication increases maintenance cost. A small concrete example shows how to pass nginx_port directly in a role entry. Practice this with environment-specific values and remember variable precedence — play or role invocation variables override defaults. Question to consider: how would you troubleshoot a role if the expected override is not applied? Passing Arguments to Roles means use role invocation variables to configure behavior per run and avoid changing role internals.. In practical terms, how to override defaults and tailor a role per invocation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding where a variable comes from is essential to predict role behavior. Ansible applies variable precedence rules so values defined closer to execution override broader defaults. A role’s defaults are intentionally low-precedence so a playbook can override them without changing the role. You can set variables at the play level, inventory, extra-vars, or pass them on the role line. For instance, defaults/main. yml might set service_state to started, but a playbook or inline role invocation can set service_state to stopped for a particular run. A practical misconception is expecting defaults to win; they are the lowest priority. When troubleshooting, examine where the variable was defined and whether an extra-vars value or play-level var is shadowing it. In complex projects, documenting which variables are intended to be overridden helps other authors. A concrete walkthrough uses the flexible_service role defaults and the test playbook to show how install_package and service_name change the role's actions. Variable Precedence and Scope means role defaults are lowest precedence; play or invocation vars override them to shape runtime behavior.. In practical terms, defaults, play vars, and role-level overrides. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Conditional logic is the primary tool to adapt tasks to the target environment. The when statement can be applied to single tasks, to whole blocks, or when including a role. A common use is branching on ansible_os_family to install the correct package name for the platform. You can also conditionally enable features, for example running firewall configuration only if firewall_enabled is truthy. A common misconception is to rely on implicit assumptions about facts; always validate the fact key you use. When combined with defaults and role arguments, when gives you precise control: a role can accept a variable feature_enabled and skip feature setup when false. A concrete example shows three tasks: installing nginx on Debian, installing on RedHat, and configuring a firewall only when a flag is set. If you see both package tasks attempting to run, check that your when expressions are correct and that facts are gathered or available. Closing question: how would you test conditionals in a CI environment where facts might differ? Conditional Logic inside Roles with when means use when everywhere needed so roles run only the tasks appropriate to each host's facts and configuration.. In practical terms, use host facts and variables to run tasks selectively. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

You can apply conditional logic not only to tasks but to the invocation of roles themselves. Putting a when on a role in the roles list or on an include_role allows you to skip entire role runs when preconditions aren't met. This is useful for toggling features across environments or preventing an expensive role from running on control nodes. A typical pattern is to set deploy_app: true in a playbook and then attach the when to the role invocation so the role is executed only when requested. A common misunderstanding is to believe conditions on roles behave exactly like task-level when clauses; role-level when checks whether to include the whole role, while task-level when controls individual steps inside the role. For orchestration, use role-level when when you want to avoid evaluating or loading a role at all. As an exercise, try adding a when: deploy_app condition to a role invocation and verify that tasks inside the role do not run when the condition is false. Guarding Role Execution with when means applying when to role invocation prevents a role from being loaded or executed when conditions are not met.. In practical terms, skip or include roles based on variables and host facts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A key design decision is picking import_role or include_role. import_role is static: Ansible processes it at parse time and effectively inlines the role's tasks into the playbook before execution begins. That means syntax errors surface early and the full task list is known ahead of running plays. It’s appropriate for predictable, fixed dependencies where you don’t need runtime decisions. include_role is dynamic: it is processed at runtime and allows looped inclusion and conditional logic evaluated during execution. That makes it the right tool when you need to include the same role multiple times with different arguments, or include depending on runtime facts. A common pitfall is using include_role when a static import would be safer; this can delay failure detection until execution reaches the include. A concrete scenario where include_role is necessary is when looping over multiple app specs and including the same role per item with different parameters for each application. When choosing, weigh early error detection and predictability versus runtime flexibility. import_role vs include_role means use import_role for static, predictable includes; use include_role when you need runtime decisions or loops.. In practical terms, static parse-time embedding vs runtime inclusion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dynamic inclusion shines when you must apply the same role multiple times with different parameters. include_role evaluated at runtime can be placed inside a task loop, letting you pass per-item vars by using loop_control and a loop variable. For example, you could loop over application specifications and include the deploy_app role for each app, setting app_name and app_port from the loop item. This pattern is ideal when the number of items or their configuration is not known until execution, or when each item needs slight variations. A misconception is trying to use import_role in a loop; static import is evaluated before the loop context exists and will not give you per-item behavior. When using include_role in loops, be mindful of idempotence and variable scoping, and prefer explicit loop_var names to avoid accidental overwrites. Try this pattern to deploy two apps with different ports using the same role and verify each run receives its own variables during execution. Dynamic Inclusion with include_role and Loops means use include_role within a loop to invoke a role multiple times with different arguments for each item.. In practical terms, deploy multiple items by including the same role per iteration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Blocks let you group tasks that share common attributes and provide structured error handling. pre_tasks and post_tasks provide a way to run global setup or teardown steps around role execution. pre_tasks execute before any roles or regular tasks, which makes them suitable for environment preparation like ensuring required packages or fetching credentials. post_tasks run after all roles and regular tasks, which is useful for cleanup, reporting, or collecting logs. A misconception is that pre_tasks replace role responsibilities; they are complementary. Use pre_tasks for global concerns that apply across roles, and keep role internals focused on their specific service domain. For example, a pre_task might ensure a package repository is configured before roles that install packages run, and a post_task might collect status or remove temporary credentials. When applying these advanced role techniques, watch for common pitfalls. One frequent mistake is duplicating a role for environment differences rather than passing arguments; duplication increases maintenance and leads to inconsistent behavior. Another is forgetting variable precedence — assuming defaults override play vars when the opposite is true — so document intended override points. Choosing include_role when you don't need runtime flexibility can hide syntax errors until execution; prefer import_role for stable, known dependencies because it surfaces parse-time problems. Also avoid placing expensive operations inside repeated includes without idempotence checks. When using when conditions, ensure the facts you reference are available; for example, gather_facts must be on or you must supply the needed facts. Best practices: keep roles focused, document overridable variables in defaults with comments, prefer import_role for static dependencies, and use include_role for per-item loops or runtime decisions. These three ideas summarize what to take away. First, role arguments let you adapt a role at invocation so one role serves many environments. Second, conditional logic using when enables precise control over which tasks or roles run based on host facts or variables. Third, import_role is parsed statically while include_role executes at runtime; choose between early error detection and runtime flexibility depending on your needs. Keeping these principles in mind helps you write modular, maintainable automation: define safe defaults in roles, override them at the play or role invocation level, guard behavior with conditionals, and use inclusion types that match your orchestration needs.
